string.text: The route leads to the NPC your task points you at. Needs "Quest targets" on the Nameplates page.
Master switch for the whole mod.
Shows and hides nameplates. Unbound (the default) means always shown.

How the key acts. Press, double tap and long press toggle nameplates on and off; their timings come from MCM's own Key Binds page. "Hold to show" keeps them up only while the key is held. Detection keeps running while they are hidden, so nothing is rescanned when they return.
The hotkey needs MCM 1.6.0 or newer. Until then nameplates are always shown.

Fades nameplates and waypoint markers down while the weapon is busy, so they sit out of the way of the sights. Triggered by aiming, firing, taking fire, reloading and clearing a jam; this is how long it lasts after the last of those. Aiming holds the fade until the sights come down. 0 turns the whole feature off. Default 15 (1.5s).
How far down they fade, as a percentage of normal. They stay readable rather than disappearing, so nothing pops in and out mid-firefight. 0 hides them completely. Default 35.
Include the NPC nameplates in the fade. Default on.
Include the through-wall waypoint markers in the fade. Default on.

During an emission and inside a psi zone, the overlay stops holding still: the marks tear sideways in bands, their outlines separate into a coloured fringe, the range readout starts printing the wrong digit, and at the worst of it the whole thing drops out for a beat at a time. It builds and fades with the emission itself, eases off when you are under cover, and settles as soon as you are clear. Default on.

How hard it pushes. Scales how far the marks move and how wide the colour fringe gets; it does not change the order the effects arrive in. Below about 50 the tear stops being visible on a low-resolution screen. Default 100.

At the very peak of an emission or a strong psi field, allow the overlay to stop drawing altogether instead of fading to a faint floor. Atmospheric, but a marker that is gone looks exactly like a marker that failed, so it is off by default and the marks stay just visible instead. Default off.
Metres of path between direction marks. Shared by both route views: it also sets how dense the minimap trail is. Default 3.
Slides the route marks toward your objective instead of holding them on fixed ground. 0 is off. 15 is a walking pace; past 40 the run reads as a flicker. Default 0.

Replace the PDA map and minimap spot icons, and the PDA symbols legend, with this mod's own. Off keeps whatever the rest of your setup draws. The game reads icon definitions once at startup, so a change applies at the next launch, not on loading a save.

How this mod's map icons are drawn. Colourised circles are the ring-and-glyph marks, one colour per role. STALKER 2 style is a white glyph in a white diamond, so a service is told apart by its glyph alone and the frame no longer says whether a marker is a person, a place to search or a job to hand in. Most colour coding goes: squad dots keep their faction colours either way, and so do a finished job's green, a bounty's red and a mutant hunt's olive. Read once at startup, like the option above, so a change applies at the next launch.

How big task markers are drawn on the PDA map and the HUD minimap, as a percentage of this mod's own size. 100 is unchanged; 67 is about a third smaller. It covers the task family only - both story tiers, the turn-in and timed pins, the new-task pulse and the hunt, bounty, delivery and hand-in marks - and leaves the service badges, squad dots and level transitions where they are. The selection ring scales with the marker it frames. Read once at startup like the two rows above, so a change applies at the next launch.

How big the service badges are drawn on the PDA map and the HUD minimap, as a percentage of this mod's own size. 100 is unchanged; 67 is about a third smaller. It covers the eight badges this mod draws - medic, trader, bed, mechanic, barman, companion, important character and quest NPC - on both views, and leaves the task markers, squad dots and level transitions to their own settings. Separate from the task slider because the two crowd different things: task pins crowd the route you are walking, badges crowd the hub you are standing in. Read once at startup, so a change applies at the next launch.

How big the level-transition arch is drawn, as a percentage of this mod's own size. 100 is unchanged. It covers all nine elements at once - the eight compass variants the PDA map picks between and the single minimap mark - because nobody reads them as nine separate marks. It has a row of its own because this is the one mark whose size is doing navigation rather than identification: it is how you find the way out of a level you do not know. Read once at startup, so a change applies at the next launch.

A skull on a mutant hunt, a red reticle on a bounty. Both return to the plain task marker once the objective is done and the job only needs handing in. Applies immediately, and turning it off puts every marker back. Needs "Enable icons".
Hunt and bounty colours (restart for pins)

Colour of the mutant hunt and bounty marks. The default bounty red is dark - 1.2:1 contrast against the map background - which is the usual reason to change it. Each preset moves both marks off the axis that deficiency collapses, keeping them apart from each other and from the other task marks. Custom uses the six sliders below, which start on the default colours. The world marker updates immediately; map and minimap pins are parsed at startup and change at the next launch.
Red channel of the mutant hunt colour (0-255). Used only when the setting above is Custom. Default 176, the shipped lime's own red.
Green channel of the mutant hunt colour (0-255). Used only when the setting above is Custom. Default 216.
Blue channel of the mutant hunt colour (0-255). Used only when the setting above is Custom. Default 72.

Red channel of the bounty colour (0-255). Used only when the setting above is Custom. Default 172. If you are changing it because the default is hard to see, raise lightness rather than saturation: a brighter red at the same lightness collides with the finished-job green under red-green deficiency.
Green channel of the bounty colour (0-255). Used only when the setting above is Custom. Default 60.
Blue channel of the bounty colour (0-255). Used only when the setting above is Custom. Default 66.

Put an NPC's own name in the tooltip you get by hovering their pin on the PDA map, alongside what they do: traders, technicians, bartenders, medics, guides and important characters. Applies immediately, and turning it off puts the plain wording back.

Your own companions keep drawing the ordinary faction squad dot on the PDA map and the minimap, a step behind your own arrow, telling you where somebody you are walking with is. This takes it off. Every other squad in the Zone is untouched. Applies immediately, and turning it off puts the dots straight back.
Write IQM debug lines to the console and log. For troubleshooting.
NPCs a task points you at: the "go talk to X" step and the turn-in.
The stalker currently asking to be escorted. Only one offers it at a time. Read from the guide job's own dialogue condition, so it matches exactly when that option is available.
Friendly stalkers you can recruit for free right now: in a squad, and within your companion limit. Uses the game's own recruit-dialogue checks, so the nameplate matches when that option is available.

Stalkers who will take money to escort you, the paid version of the companion dialogue. Genuinely rare: only neutral stalkers, only from Loners, Freedom, Mercenaries and Bandits, only veteran and advanced squads, never on the dangerous maps or under Warfare. A stalker without one is not a detection failure.
NPCs offering fast travel. Read from the PDA map-spot registry, so it always matches the map legend.

Traders, technicians, barkeeps and medics, each with its own header and glyph. The trade is read from the NPC's actual trade file, so a technician the level labels as a trader still shows the technician glyph.
Story and faction VIPs, the ones your PDA marks with the Important Character icon. Off by default: busy hubs already show plenty.

Friendly stalkers who would offer you a task if you asked, with the job kind when known ("HIRING: BOUNTY"). No nameplate means "Nothing at the moment". Experimental: this queries the task system, a heavy lookup the base game only runs when a dialogue or the taskboard opens. Checks are cached and rationed, but turn it off if camps stutter.
Tint the nameplate with the NPC's faction colour instead of the accent. Factionless NPCs keep the accent.
Show the NPC's faction patch on quest, guide, companion and hire nameplates. Service and VIP nameplates keep their role glyph instead.
How service and VIP nameplates are drawn. Icon chip is a compact plate with just the glyph.
"Senior Sergeant Abdurakhmanov" becomes "Snr Sgt Abdurakhmanov". Only the leading rank is shortened.
Range at which the nameplate starts to fade in. Hidden beyond it.
Hide the nameplate when the NPC is behind cover. Needs the shared demonized_geometry_ray utility (bundled with many GAMMA mods); without it this has no effect.

Fade out nameplates away from the centre of the screen, so only the person you are looking at is named. Off shows every nameplate at once, as before. Ambient only leaves the objective, guide, recruit and hire nameplates always visible and focuses the service and HIRING ones. All but objective also focuses the guide, recruit and hire nameplates. Everything focuses the objective too.

How far from the crosshair a nameplate still counts as focused, as a percentage of half the screen height -- the same scale as the waypoint markers' centre falloff, so 50 here is the same circle as 50 there. Aiming down sights narrows what this covers in the world, since the view is magnified into the same circle.
How much of the radius is a fade rather than a boundary. 0 makes nameplates pop as they cross the edge; 100 fades from the very centre outward.
How visible a nameplate outside the circle stays. 0 hides it completely; raise it to quieten the rest of the screen rather than clear it.
Beep the first time each NPC's nameplate comes into view. A per-NPC cooldown stops brief glances re-triggering it.
Master alpha of the accent: line, edge bar, header and node.
Red channel of the accent (0-255). Default 224.
Green channel of the accent (0-255). Default 196.
Blue channel of the accent (0-255). Default 122, a soft desaturated gold.
Horizontal distance from the head to the nameplate. It flips side automatically near the screen edge.
How far above the head the nameplate floats.
Opacity of the dark plate at full visibility (0-255).
Draw the dot at the NPC where the leader line begins.
Slowly breathe the halo around the node. The dot itself stays steady.
Full size of the node dot, reached inside the full-opacity distance.
How small the dot shrinks at the appear distance, as a fraction of full size. 1.0 = no distance scaling.
Thickness of the leader line from the node to the nameplate.
Opacity of the leader line at full visibility (0-255).
Nudge the node up (+) or down (-) from the NPC's shoulder bone. 0 sits on the shoulder near the neck.
Nudge the node along the NPC's own body axis, right (+) or left (-). Tracks their facing. Added on top of the auto placement below.
Put the node on whichever shoulder is on the nameplate's side of the screen, so the leader line does not cross the NPC's body.
How far onto the shoulder the auto placement pushes the node, roughly a torso half-width.
How quickly the nameplate eases toward the NPC. 1 = instant, lower = smoother but laggier. Framerate-independent. Default 0.35.
Position jumps larger than this teleport instead of gliding, so the nameplate does not slide across the screen when the NPC first appears.
Inside this range the nameplate is solid; between it and the appear distance it fades. Keep it below the appear distance.
How often each NPC's line of sight is re-tested. Lower reacts faster and costs more. Default 150.
How long the nameplate lingers after cover breaks line of sight, to stop flicker from doorways and passing objects. 0 hides instantly. Default 250.

Query the task system for NPCs with no known answer yet, at most one every 0.3 s, nearest first. This does what opening their dialogue does, just earlier: their offered task is decided when the nameplate appears rather than when you talk. Off makes the detector passive, showing only NPCs the game has already decided.

The objective of the task you picked on the PDA, the one your map draws a bracket around. Drawn through walls, and parked at the screen edge when it is behind you. Carries the same reticle that marker wears on the map. There is only ever one: change the selection and it follows, and with nothing selected nothing is marked. Shows at any range, and works for an objective that is not an NPC. Needs "Quest targets".
Only when ready to hand in

Mark the selected task only once its objective is done and the marker has moved to whoever you report back to. On by default. This is a difficulty setting: at the earlier stages the marker is an exact live position through a wall, so on a bounty it hands you the part of the task that was the challenge. Turn it off to have the marker follow the objective at every stage. Either way the ground route still leads to the objective.
Every hand-in, not just the selected one

Mark everyone who is waiting on a finished job of yours, not only the task you picked on the PDA. On by default, and it is what decides whether a turn-in outranks a shop on the same person: with this off the hand-in role carries no marker, so the marker falls to whatever else that NPC is -- trader, technician, barkeep, medic -- and you get REPORT BACK on the card with a trader glyph through the wall. Rides the distance below, unlike your selected task. Needs "Quest targets".

Range of the guide and service markers above. Meant to find someone you are already near, not to navigate the map. Never drops below the appear distance. Your selected task and your own waypoint ignore it and show at any range. Default 60.
Also mark fast-travel guides. Off by default.
Also mark traders, technicians, barkeeps and medics, each with its PDA map glyph. Off by default.

Mark the waypoint you placed with Personal Adjustable Waypoint, carrying the same ring your PDA map draws. The one marker with no distance limit, since you chose the position. Hidden once you are standing on it.

Also mark the companions travelling with you, wearing the same bust your PDA map puts on them. Off by default. They are the last thing offered a slot, so a companion can never push a quest turn-in or a shop off the screen, and they use the guide / service distance above.

What tints the marker. Map icon gives each one the colour its PDA map spot carries, so the colour you learn on the map is the colour you look for through the wall. The third option is the same, except turn-ins take the quest giver's faction colour. Custom puts every marker on its own colour, set by the three channels in Advanced below, and leaves the nameplates on the accent. Guides and your own waypoint always keep the accent.
Show the distance in metres under the glyph.
Height of the metre figures, as a percentage of the marker size. Default 40.

Print the NPC's name above the marker. Off by default: the name is the one part that cannot follow the size slider, because the engine draws text at a fixed size picked from your resolution. Near the default marker size the two agree.
Glyph size on the badge. The badge, arrow and spacing all scale from it, so it is the one knob for overall marker size. Default 14.
How far in from the screen edge an off-screen marker parks. Larger keeps it clear of the HUD corners.
Opacity of the marker and its range readout (0-255).

Red channel of the marker's own colour (0-255). Used only with Colour set to Custom above; the accent is used otherwise. Default 224, the accent's own red, so Custom starts where the gold is and you shift it from there.
Green channel of the marker's own colour (0-255). Default 196.
Blue channel of the marker's own colour (0-255). Default 122. The badge keyline is artwork and is not tinted, so a dark colour keeps its edge against sky.

Shrink and fade a marker as it nears the crosshair, so it gets out of the way of whatever you are looking at. The value is the radius, as a percentage of half your screen height: 35 reaches about a sixth of the screen height out from the crosshair, 100 reaches the top and bottom edges. Applies only to markers on screen (one parked at an edge is already far from the centre), and never to the waypoint you placed yourself, which is meant to sit dead centre while you walk to it. 0 turns the feature off. Default 35.

How far down a marker fades at the very centre, as a percentage of normal. It stays visible rather than disappearing, so nothing pops in and out as you turn. 0 hides it completely. The size floor is fixed and much shallower (three quarters), because a badge shrunk further stops reading as a glyph. Default 20.

Whether a marker near the centre also gets smaller, or only fades. On by default. Turn it off to keep every marker at its normal size, so your eye does not have to find it again as it changes. The fade cannot be switched off here; set Centre falloff to 0 for that.

Draw a line along the ground to your selected task's target, with chevrons for direction. Follows walkable terrain and fades behind cover. Select another task in the PDA and it follows. With no task selected it falls back to the nearest objective NPC. Needs "Quest targets".

"Summoned" is the default: the line appears while you hold the key, holds for a moment after you let go, then fades. Nothing is recalculated when it comes back, so summoning it repeatedly is free. "Follow nameplates" draws it whenever the nameplates are up. "Always" ignores the key entirely.
How long the line stays up after the key comes up, before it fades. This is what lets a tap work rather than making you hold the key down. 0 fades it the moment you let go. Default 20 (2.0s).

The key that summons the route. Unbound (the default) borrows the nameplate key, where a tap will also toggle the nameplates; give the route its own key and it stops touching them, so you can leave nameplates up and pulse the route on its own.
Summoned needs a key: bind one here, or the nameplate hotkey on the General page. Until then the route is drawn all the time.
How much of the line is drawn, measured along the path from where you stand. Not a limit on how far the target may be. The minimap trail has its own distance. Default 50.

Which mark is painted on the floor. All three point the way. Arrowhead is a solid triangle and the widest. It also sits flattest on uneven ground, because each mark is drawn as a single quad and a shallower shape matches the ground better. The chevrons trade some of that for a sharper point. The small one reads as a tick at distance. Costs nothing either way. Default Chevron - large.

Make the marks on the ground brighten and dim, as a wave that travels along the route towards your objective, so the pulse carries direction the same way the marks do. It only ever brightens: at the bottom of each cycle a mark sits at exactly the colour you set, so your route colour is unchanged. Marks are drawn over the scene rather than in it, so this cannot light the ground or bloom. The amount scales with how much room your colour has left to brighten, so it stays visible on dark and light colours alike. At 10 a mark reaches as bright as that colour goes. 0 turns it off. Default 6.
Opacity of the line and its chevrons (0-255). Stretches behind cover draw at a fraction of this.
Red channel of the route colour (0-255). Default 176, a light olive picked to sit in the scene without disappearing into the ground.
Green channel of the route colour (0-255). Default 196.
Blue channel of the route colour (0-255). Default 124.
Fade the stretches behind walls and rises instead of hiding them. Recommended on: the interesting part of a route is usually the part going round something. The minimap trail is unaffected.

Show the route as a trail of marks on the HUD minimap. Independent of the ground line: either, both or neither. With both on they agree, being two views of one route. Better than the ground line when the route is behind a building, and the only one that works if your setup cannot draw the world-space line at all.
How much of the route the trail covers, measured along the path. Separate from the ground line's distance, and cheap to raise since both views come from one route. Default 50.
Arrows point the way the route goes. Dots are quieter on a cluttered map. Costs nothing either way. Default Arrows.
Size of each trail mark. The minimap is small, so this range is too: at the top a single mark is a tenth of the map's width. Default 8.

Red channel of the trail colour (0-255). Separate from the ground route's, since this is read off a map against terrain and other mods' spots. White by default. The black outline is artwork and is not tinted.
Green channel of the trail colour (0-255).
Blue channel of the trail colour (0-255).
